in_text_mentions: Chagas disease refers to the infection by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by the bite of species of Triatoma, also known as the kissing bug. The disease plagued South America at a pandemic scale during the early 20th century [1]. At that time, a few researchers devoted themselves to this infection, like Carlos Chagas, Emmanuel Dias, Emile Roubaud, or even Cecilio Romaña (Fig 1). The latter described the transmission pathway through the conjunctiva that leads to periorbital painless swelling, which is known as the Romaña’s sign and indicates acute Chagas disease (Fig 2) [2].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Low-power H&E histology from a skin punch biopsy of a patient with Chagas disease reactivation, demonstrating a deep dermal to subcutaneous inflammatory infiltrate, a cutaneous manifestation of the disease. B: Medium-power H&E histology from the same skin biopsy, demonstrating medium-vessel vasculitis (marked by arrow) and lobular panniculitis, consistent with Chagas disease reactivation-associated cutaneous vasculitis. C: High-magnification H&E histology demonstrating intracellular protozoal amastigotes, a pathognomonic finding for Chagas disease, confirming the diagnosis of reactivation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: HE skin biopsy showing lobular panniculitis with neutrophilic infiltrate. The disease-focused article title identifies the thigh lobular panniculitis as the cutaneous manifestation of reactivated Chagas disease; in-text ties the same biopsy to T. cruzi amastigotes. No matching vocabulary key for panniculitis, so findings are placed in proposed_findings. B: High-power HE of the Chagas reactivation skin biopsy directly showing intracellular microorganisms morphologically consistent with T. cruzi amastigotes, matching the allowed histology finding for intracellular amastigote pseudocysts.
